books.title: Mansfield Park
books.author: Jane Austen
books.desc: Sent at ten to live with rich relations, shy Fanny Price grows up quietly watching the Bertram family, until the dazzling Crawfords arrive and test everyone's principles.
about: At the age of ten, Fanny Price is sent away from her large, struggling family to live at Mansfield Park, the grand house of her wealthy uncle and aunt, Sir Thomas and Lady Bertram. Timid and often overlooked, she finds a friend in her cousin Edmund. When Sir Thomas leaves to attend to his estate in Antigua, the lively Henry and Mary Crawford arrive in the neighbourhood, and the young people of the house throw themselves into flirtation and a scheme of amateur theatricals that Fanny watches with growing unease.

Austen sets charm against principle and asks what kind of upbringing makes a good person. Fanny is a quiet, steadfast heroine rather than a witty one, and the novel's irony falls on the vanity, idleness and selfishness around her. The family's wealth rests partly on a plantation in Antigua, worked by enslaved people in the period, a link the novel touches on only briefly but which modern readers have discussed at length.

Written at Chawton between 1812 and 1814, Mansfield Park was Austen's third published novel and appeared in 1814 from Thomas Egerton. It has long divided readers over its serious heroine, and it remains one of the most debated of her books. It has been adapted for film, including a 1999 version, and for television.

books.title: The Woman in White
books.author: Wilkie Collins
books.desc: A drawing master meets a mysterious woman dressed in white on a moonlit road, and is drawn into a conspiracy of stolen identity, money and marriage.
about: Walking back to London late one night, the young drawing master Walter Hartright meets a strange woman dressed all in white who has escaped from an asylum. Soon afterwards he takes up a post at Limmeridge House in Cumberland, teaching the gentle Laura Fairlie and her clever, resolute half-sister Marian Halcombe. Walter is startled by Laura's likeness to the woman in white, and troubled to learn that Laura is engaged to the baronet Sir Percival Glyde.

Collins tells the story through a series of narrators, each giving evidence in turn as witnesses would in a court of law. The book mixes suspense, secrets and false identities with a pointed look at how little power the law gave a married woman over her own fortune. Marian Halcombe and the charming, sinister Count Fosco are among the most memorable characters in Victorian fiction.

The novel was serialised in Charles Dickens's weekly All the Year Round from 26 November 1859 to 25 August 1860 and published in book form in 1860. It made Collins famous and is generally regarded as the starting point of the sensation novel, as well as one of the first mystery novels in English. Collins adapted it for the stage in 1871.

books.title: North and South
books.author: Elizabeth Gaskell
books.desc: Uprooted from a quiet southern village to a smoky northern mill town, Margaret Hale clashes with the proud factory owner John Thornton as workers and masters collide.
about: Margaret Hale has grown up between her aunt's elegant house in Harley Street, London, and her father's country parsonage at Helstone in Hampshire. When her father leaves the Church of England for reasons of conscience, the family moves to Milton, a crowded manufacturing town in the north. There Margaret meets John Thornton, a proud, self-made cotton-mill owner, and the two take an instant dislike to each other just as tension grows between the mill owners and their workers.

Gaskell, who lived in Manchester, sets the values of the rural south against those of the industrial north and gives a voice to masters and workers alike. Strikes, poverty, illness and the question of what employers owe the people they employ are at the heart of the story, alongside a slowly developing relationship between two strong-willed people who must learn to understand each other.

The novel was serialised weekly in Household Words from 2 September 1854 to 27 January 1855 and published in two volumes in 1855. Gaskell wanted to call it Margaret Hale, but Charles Dickens, the magazine's editor, insisted on North and South. It is now counted among the finest Victorian novels about industrial England.
books.author_short: English novelist and biographer (1810–1865), author of Mary Barton, Cranford, North and South and The Life of Charlotte Brontë.
author_long: Elizabeth Cleghorn Stevenson was born on 29 September 1810 in Chelsea, London. Her mother died when she was a baby, and she was brought up by an aunt in Knutsford, Cheshire, a small town that later inspired her fiction. In 1832 she married William Gaskell, a Unitarian minister at Cross Street Chapel in Manchester, where the couple lived and raised their family. After the death of their infant son, she turned to writing. She died suddenly on 12 November 1865 at Holybourne in Hampshire, aged 55.

Her first novel, Mary Barton (1848), described the lives of the Manchester poor and made her name. It was followed by Cranford and Ruth (both 1853), North and South (1855), the pioneering biography The Life of Charlotte Brontë (1857), Sylvia's Lovers (1863) and Wives and Daughters, left unfinished at her death and published in 1866. Cranford and North and South first appeared in Household Words, the magazine edited by Charles Dickens.

books.title: Silas Marner
books.author: George Eliot
books.desc: Betrayed and cast out, a lonely weaver hoards gold in a quiet village, until one winter night his treasure vanishes and a golden-haired child appears at his door.
about: Silas Marner is a weaver and a devout member of a small chapel congregation at Lantern Yard, in a town in the north of England. Falsely accused of theft, betrayed by his closest friend and abandoned by his fiancée, he loses his faith and moves to the village of Raveloe. There he lives alone for fifteen years, working at his loom and finding comfort only in the gold coins he earns. Meanwhile, at the Red House, the squire's sons Godfrey and Dunstan Cass have secrets of their own.

Eliot tells a story close to a fable, about loss, trust and the way love and community can bring a broken life back into the world. She paints village life with warmth and humour, catching the talk of its inhabitants at the local inn, while showing how chance, conscience and choice shape people's fates.

Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe, Eliot's third novel, was published on 2 April 1861 by William Blackwood and Sons. Short and accessible, it became one of her most widely read works and has long been studied in schools. The Spanish translation offered here, by an unnamed translator, was published in Buenos Aires in 1919 by the Biblioteca de La Nación.

books.title: Far from the Madding Crowd
books.author: Thomas Hardy
books.desc: Independent Bathsheba Everdene runs her own farm in rural Wessex and must choose between a loyal shepherd, a lonely neighbour and a dashing soldier.
about: Gabriel Oak, a young shepherd, proposes to the spirited Bathsheba Everdene and is turned down. When misfortune ruins him, he finds work on the farm she has just inherited at Weatherbury, where she decides to manage everything herself. Soon her attention is sought by two very different men: William Boldwood, a serious and solitary gentleman farmer next door, and Sergeant Frank Troy, a charming and reckless soldier.

Hardy follows the farming year, from lambing and sheep-shearing to harvest and storms, and fills the story with the humour of the farm workers who comment on events. Through Bathsheba, a woman running her own business in a man's world, he explores love, pride, loyalty and the part that chance plays in people's lives.

The novel first appeared anonymously as a monthly serial in the Cornhill Magazine and was published in book form on 23 November 1874. It was Hardy's fourth published novel and his first major success, and it introduced the name Wessex for his fictional region of south-west England. The title comes from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard. It has been filmed several times, including Thomas Vinterberg's 2015 version.
